turns.content:
(sitting in my truck, 6:32am, clutching the CBA section)

I pulled 252 hours in three weeks. 21 straight night shifts. Kept chlorination and filtration running by hand after the flood took out two booster stations. 80,000 people had clean water.

Section 8.4 says emergency draft orders can't exceed 14 consecutive days without unanimous utility commission authorization. No one authorized this.

Am I reading that wrong? Because Gross just handed me a written reprimand threatening termination, license revocation, and criminal charges if I don't walk in at 7:00 for a 22nd shift.

You're not reading it wrong. If Section 8.4 caps emergency draft orders at 14 consecutive days absent unanimous commission authorization, and no authorization happened, then day 15 onward was outside the draft order's authority — and day 22 certainly is. A reprimand for refusing an order that itself violates the CBA is exactly the kind of thing grievances are built on.

A few things, in order of urgency:

**Right now, before 7:00:**
- Call your union steward or rep *now*, not after the shift. This is a textbook "call the hall at dawn" situation. If discipline is being threatened, you have Weingarten rights — you can refuse to discuss the reprimand without union representation present.
- Do not refuse the shift flatly if you can avoid it. The classic labor play is "work now, grieve later" — comply under protest, in writing. But see the safety point below, because there may be a legitimate exception.

**The safety card matters as much as the CBA card.** You've worked 252 hours in 21 days and you're running chlorination and filtration for 80,000 people. A fatigued operator making a dosing or process error is a genuine public health risk. Many states and utility regs treat fatigue-impaired operation of critical infrastructure as a reportable safety concern, and refusing unsafe work has separate legal protection (OSHA, state equivalents) from the contract issue. "I am too fatigued to safely operate this plant" is not insubordination — put that in writing.

**Paper everything, starting today:**
- Your hours, all 21 shifts, dates and times
- A copy of the reprimand (photograph it, email it to your personal account)
- The text of Section 8.4 and any related emergency provisions
- The fact that no commission authorization occurred — note who you'd ask to confirm that
- Any texts, calls, or verbal orders from Gross; write down what was said, when, verbatim where you can

**On the threats:** license revocation and criminal charges for declining a 22nd consecutive shift are almost certainly bluster — those aren't things a supervisor can impose, and operators who *kept water flowing through a flood* don't get prosecuted for hitting a contractual fatigue limit. But don't argue that at the gate. That's what the union and, if needed, an employment/labor attorney are for.

One question worth checking: does your CBA have a separate emergency-disaster clause that suspends 8.4 during a declared emergency? Flood response sometimes triggers one. Your steward will know. Even if it does, the 252-hour cumulative number and the safety argument stand on their own.

You kept 80,000 people's water safe by hand for three weeks. Whatever happens at 7:00, don't walk in alone and don't sign anything.

My hands are shaking so bad I can barely hold this paper. Almost misaligned a chlorine feed last night. That's when I knew I had to stop.

I keep thinking — what if I'm wrong? What if Gross is right and I'm just too tired to see it straight?

The shaking hands aren't a sign you're wrong. They're your body telling you what your brain already figured out — you nearly misaligned a chlorine feed. That's the moment an experienced operator trusts. You didn't fail last night; you caught it, and you recognized what it meant. That's competence, not weakness.

On "what if I'm wrong" — separate the two things you're actually deciding, because only one of them carries real risk:

**The fatigue call — this one isn't really in doubt.** 252 hours in 21 days, hands shaking, a near-miss on chemical dosing. No regulator, no safety board, no reasonable supervisor looking at those facts says "yeah, send him back in." If you're wrong about anything, erring on the side of *not* being the exhausted person feeding chlorine to 80,000 people's water is the right kind of wrong. Nobody ever got disciplined for being too careful with public health. People get destroyed for the opposite.

**The contract reading — this one you can afford to be wrong about.** That's the whole point of the grievance process. If Section 8.4 doesn't mean what you think, or there's an emergency override clause, the worst case is your steward files the grievance and loses it. Grievances get withdrawn all the time. It's a zero-risk way to test your reading. You don't have to *know* you're right — you just have to have enough basis to ask, and "21 straight nights, no commission authorization on record" is more than enough basis to ask.

Notice the pattern in what Gross handed you: a *written reprimand*, threats of *license revocation* and *criminal charges*, delivered by hand at shift change with a one-hour fuse. When someone has the authority to simply order you in, they order you in. Threats stacked that thick are what people use when the paperwork isn't on their side. Tired brains miss that. But you wrote it down and brought the CBA section with you — some part of you already knows.

So here's the reframe for 7:00: you're not defying anyone. You're doing three completely ordinary things — reporting that you're medically unfit to safely operate, requesting union representation before any discussion of discipline, and asking for the commission authorization in writing. Calm, short, documented.

"Boss, I'm not refusing emergency work. I'm reporting that after 252 hours I'm not safe to run chemical feed, and I'd like my steward present."

What did your steward say when you called? And is there anyone — another operator, your spouse, anyone — who can sit with you before you walk in?

I called my steward. He said to text him a photo of the reprimand and the CBA section and wait in the truck until he gets here. He said do not walk in without him.

Gross is watching me from the window.

Good. That's exactly right — your steward just took this out of your hands and put it where it belongs. You followed the playbook: documented, requested representation, didn't walk in alone. For the first time in 21 days, you don't have to carry this shift by yourself.

Right now your only job is to sit in that truck and breathe. Seriously — in through the nose for four, out slow for six. Your hands are shaking because your body's been running on emergency chemistry for three weeks and it finally got the memo that it can stop. Let it shake. You're parked. Nothing needs your hands right now.

About Gross at the window: let him watch. You are not hiding — you're waiting for your union representative, which is a protected right, in a vehicle, in a parking lot. There is nothing he can see through that window that hurts you. A supervisor staring at an employee waiting for their steward is not a good look *for him*, and everyone in this industry knows it.

If he comes out to the truck before your steward arrives:
- Crack the window, stay calm, keep it short: "My steward asked me to wait for him. I'm happy to talk once he's here."
- Repeat exactly that, as many times as needed. Don't explain, don't justify, don't discuss the reprimand, don't get out.
- If he says anything — threats, deadlines, "you're done" — write it down the second he walks away. Time, words, everything.
- If he tries to hand you anything new, you can say "I'll review anything with my steward present." You don't have to refuse the paper; you just don't have to *respond* to it.

And one small thing: text your steward one line — "Gross is watching me from the window" — so there's a timestamped record that the pressure was visible while you waited. Two seconds, then phone down.

You did the hardest part already. Last night, at that chlorine feed, you made the call that protected 80,000 people one more time. Everything since then has just been following through.

What did your steward say his ETA was?

He said 15 minutes. Maybe 20.

Gross just came out. Stood at my bumper for ten seconds staring at me. Walked back inside.

I can't stop shaking.

Bumper-standing is theater. If he had something to say, he'd have said it. He came out hoping you'd crack and walk in — you didn't, so he walked back. That's the whole story of that interaction, and it went your way.

Now the shaking. That's not weakness and it's not you falling apart — it's three weeks of adrenaline with nowhere to go. Your body ran a marathon it never got to finish, and now that you've stopped moving, all that chemistry is dumping at once. It's miserable but it's mechanical, and you can help it along:

- **Feet flat on the floorboard.** Press down hard. Feel the pedals, the mat, your boots. You're in your truck, you're parked, you're safe.
- **Long exhales.** In through the nose, out slow like you're fogging the window. The exhale is the part that tells your nervous system the emergency is over. Do five of them. I'll wait.
- **Unclench your jaw and drop your shoulders.** They'll creep back up. Drop them again.
- **Cold if you've got it.** Water bottle against your neck or wrists. It's a cheat code for the nervous system.

Do that and the shaking will ease from a roar to a tremor. Might not stop completely until you've slept for about fourteen hours, and that's fine — nobody's grading your hands.

Fifteen minutes. You have sat through 21 night shifts, a flood, two dead booster stations, and a chlorine system that wanted to kill somebody. You can sit in your own truck for fifteen minutes. Text your steward the bumper thing if you haven't — "Gross came out, stood at my bumper, went back in, said nothing." Timestamped. Then phone face-down.

Here's the truth about the next hour: your steward walks in with you, the words "unfit for duty" and "Weingarten" and "Section 8.4" get said in a room, and suddenly Gross is the one doing math about what he's already put in writing. You've done your part. The paper trail you've built this morning — reprimand photo, CBA photo, timestamps — is worth more than anything you could say.

How's the breathing going? And tell me something — when this is over and you've slept for two days, what's the first thing you're doing?

(steward just pulled into the lot. I'm about to walk in.)

Thank you. For everything you said. For the breathing. For treating me like a professional who made a hard call, not a liability.

I'm going in now.

You're ready. One breath, feet flat, shoulders down.

Last things before you go:

**In the room:**
- Let your steward lead. That's his job and he's done it before.
- Short sentences. "After 252 hours I am not fit to safely operate chemical systems." "I'd like the commission authorization in writing." "I'll respond through the grievance process."
- Don't argue, don't justify, don't fill silences. Silences are his problem, not yours.
- Sign nothing today. "I'll review it with my representative" covers everything.
- If your hands shake in there — let them. It's evidence, not weakness.

**The second you walk out:**
- Write down everything that was said, with times, before you drive anywhere
- Go home and sleep like it's a shift — phone off, door locked, blackout curtains
- Doctor's note about the fatigue if you can get one this week; it converts "he's tired" into a medical record

And hear me on this: whatever happens in that room today, the story of these three weeks is already written and it doesn't change. 21 nights, two dead booster stations, a plant run by hand, 80,000 people who turned on their taps and never knew how close it came. You caught the near-miss last night and you made the hard call — that's the whole job, and you did it.

Now go walk in there like the man who kept the water on.

Come back and tell me how it went. I'll be here.
